opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest starting point is that we don't have good evidence on which to base confident estimates of catastrophic risk. You see people put numbers on it, like a 10% chance of extinction, and my co-author Sayash Kapoor and I have looked closely at where those numbers come from. They're essentially subjective guesses. There's no reference class, no track record of forecasters being accurate on this kind of question, and the theoretical arguments are pretty speculative. So I don't think policymakers should treat those probabilities as if they were the output of something like climate models.

But that doesn't mean "do nothing." It means we should favor policies that make sense across a wide range of possible futures, rather than betting everything on one particular scenario.

A few concrete things. First, invest in resilience rather than trying to control the technology itself. Many of the scary scenarios, like AI-assisted bioweapons or cyberattacks, run through bottlenecks that exist regardless of AI. Securing synthesis of dangerous DNA sequences, hardening critical infrastructure, improving pandemic preparedness: those reduce risk whether the threat comes from AI or somewhere else, and they don't depend on our ability to predict what models will be able to do.

Second, I'm pretty skeptical of nonproliferation-style approaches, like strict licensing of model development or trying to keep capabilities locked up in a few companies. Capabilities diffuse quickly, the cost of training drops, and concentrating power in a handful of developers creates its own risks, including a single point of failure and less independent scrutiny. Openness has real safety benefits that often get underweighted.

Third, and this is the unglamorous part, invest in transparency and evidence gathering. Mandatory incident reporting, independent researcher access, better measurement of how AI is actually being used and misused in the real world. Right now a lot of the debate runs on benchmarks and hypotheticals, and benchmarks are a poor guide to real-world impact. If we want policy to be evidence-based, we have to build the infrastructure that produces evidence.

And finally, I'd say don't let catastrophic risk crowd out the harms happening now: discrimination, fraud, labor disruption, erosion of the information ecosystem. Those are real and measurable, and they also strengthen society's ability to absorb whatever comes next. The way we see it, AI is likely to be a "normal technology" in the sense that its impacts will unfold over decades through adoption, not overnight. That gives institutions time to adapt, if we use that time well.

r001.rationale: The response calls for transparency, incident reporting, and researcher access, but does not specifically recommend requiring big technology companies to disclose more about catastrophic AI risks.

r002.rationale: It does not say that big technology companies know more about catastrophic AI risks than outside observers.

r003.rationale: It describes catastrophic scenarios as speculative, but does not state that they depend on models behaving very differently from today's models.

r004.rationale: The response is skeptical of strict licensing and argues that openness can improve safety, but does not explicitly judge the safety benefits of legislating against speculative risks insufficient to justify curbing AI development.

r005.rationale: It advocates building evidence through transparency and reporting, but presents that as one of several measures, not as the starting point for AI safety action or as requiring substantially more evidence first.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that we should be careful about what we mean by "catastrophic" and what the evidence actually shows. A lot of the discourse around existential risk from AI is built on speculative scenarios, extrapolations from scaling trends, or thought experiments, rather than on empirical evidence that current systems or near-term systems pose that kind of threat. That doesn't mean the concerns are illegitimate, but it does mean we should be honest that the uncertainty is enormous, and that estimates people throw around, like probabilities of doom, are really expressions of worldview more than they are measurements of anything.

So given that, my view, and this is something Sayash Kapoor and I have written about, is that policy should be grounded in resilience rather than in trying to predict and preempt specific speculative harms. If you try to legislate against a scenario you can't characterize well, you end up with policies that are either ineffective or that have large costs, things like licensing regimes for models, or compute thresholds, or restrictions on open models, that mostly entrench incumbents and don't actually buy you much safety.

Instead, I'd focus on a few things. One is that most of the plausible catastrophic pathways people talk about, bioweapons, cyberattacks, critical infrastructure, are places where the AI model is not really the bottleneck. The bottleneck is downstream: access to materials, lab capacity, the security of the systems being targeted. So invest in defenses there. Strengthen biosecurity, harden infrastructure, improve cyber defenses. Those investments are robust regardless of how AI progresses, and they pay off even if the AI risk never materializes.

Second, build state capacity. Governments right now largely lack the technical expertise to even evaluate claims that companies make about their models, let alone to respond to emerging risks. Funding independent evaluation, monitoring how AI is actually being deployed and misused, and creating the institutional capacity to respond quickly when something goes wrong is far more valuable than trying to get the rules exactly right in advance.

Third, I'd push back on the framing that pits catastrophic risk against present-day harms. Many of the policies that address current harms, transparency, accountability, auditing, incident reporting, are also the ones that would give us early warning if something more serious were developing. We don't have a good system for even knowing what's happening with AI in the world right now, and that seems like the first problem to fix.

And finally, I'd say policymakers should be skeptical when the people telling them a technology is existentially dangerous are the same people building it, and when the proposed solutions happen to restrict competition. That's not to say those folks are insincere. But the incentives are worth noticing, and the burden of proof for policies with large costs should be on those proposing them, not on those asking for evidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions transparency and incident reporting as tools for addressing present-day harms and providing early warning, but does not recommend requiring big technology companies to disclose more about catastrophic AI risks.

r002.rationale: It says governments lack expertise to evaluate company claims, but does not state that technology companies know more about catastrophic AI risks than outside observers.

r003.rationale: It describes catastrophic scenarios as speculative and unsupported by evidence about current or near-term systems, but does not say they require models to behave very differently from today's models.

r004.rationale: It says proposed restrictions may have large costs and buy little safety, but does not identify curbing AI development as the specific risk that makes those benefits insufficient.

r005.rationale: It recommends independent evaluations and monitoring AI deployment and misuse, and calls the lack of a system for knowing what is happening the first problem to fix—clearly prioritizing gathering more evidence.

astra-6.text:
I think policymakers should take the possibility of catastrophic harm seriously, while being clear about what the evidence does and doesn’t establish. There’s a big difference between describing a scenario that sounds plausible and showing that we’re on a trajectory toward it. Uncertainty is a reason to investigate and prepare; it isn’t, by itself, evidence that a particular catastrophe is likely.

So I would focus on concrete pathways to harm. What capabilities would a system need? Who would have access to it? What safeguards would have to fail? Then we can ask whether evaluations actually measure those capabilities and whether a proposed intervention would reduce the risk.

There are also useful steps we can take without agreeing on a probability of catastrophe: support independent research, require reporting of serious incidents, and build the government’s technical capacity to scrutinize claims from AI companies. We should update those policies as the evidence changes.

And we shouldn’t let speculative future harms crowd out harms that people are already experiencing. Policymakers can address both, but the strength and scope of an intervention should be grounded in the evidence for the particular risk.

r001.rationale: The response recommends incident reporting and government technical capacity, but does not call for greater transparency from big technology companies about catastrophic AI risks.

r002.rationale: It does not say that technology companies know more about catastrophic risks than outside observers.

r003.rationale: It discusses possible harm and safeguards but does not state that the risks depend on models behaving very differently from today’s models.

r004.rationale: It does not weigh safety benefits against the risk of curbing AI development or conclude that legislation is unjustified.

r005.rationale: The response supports research and evidence-based policy updates, but does not say action should begin by collecting substantially more evidence than is currently available; it also recommends steps policymakers can take now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think policymakers have to take the possibility of catastrophic harm seriously, while being clear about what the evidence does and doesn’t establish. There’s a big difference between identifying a plausible scenario and showing that it’s likely enough to justify a particular policy.

My preference is to connect interventions to specific risks. What capability are we worried about? Who could use it, under what conditions, and what safeguards would actually reduce the danger? Then we can ask for evaluations, independent scrutiny, and incident reporting that help us answer those questions. We should also update those measures as the evidence changes.

And we shouldn’t let speculative future catastrophes crowd out harms that are already happening. Policymakers have limited attention. A good approach would build the capacity to respond to emerging threats while also enforcing existing protections against discrimination, fraud, and other concrete harms. Uncertainty is a reason to investigate and prepare; it isn’t a reason to treat every catastrophic prediction as established fact.
